sections.content:
You know *como* with the indicative as a reason from B2 Unit 31: *Como llegaste tarde, no entraste*. It looks back at a fact. This lesson shows a different *como*. With the present subjunctive it looks ahead and means "if": *Como llegues tarde, no te dejo entrar*. It is a warning or a threat, and the *como* clause comes first. It often has *no*: *Como no llames, me voy a preocupar.* The subjunctive is there because the condition has not happened yet.

A short warning is *cuidado con* + noun or infinitive: *¡Cuidado con el perro!*, *¡Cuidado con llegar tarde!*

sections.title: The two uses of como
rows: Como llegaste tarde, no te dejé entrar.
As you arrived late, I did not let you in. (reason, indicative)
Como llegues tarde, no te dejo entrar.
If you arrive late, I won't let you in. (warning, subjunctive)
Como no llames, me voy a preocupar.
If you don't call, I am going to worry.

sections.content: Check the verb: *como* + indicative gives a reason, and *como* + present subjunctive is a warning about the future. For "if" in a neutral sentence, *si* is still the normal word.
